records.name: Grenada
records.summary: Grenada demands real caution. The buggery law (10 years) remains on the books (no successful court challenge yet), though unenforced; no LGR; small community; tourist areas insulated.

sources.summary: The Advocates for Human Rights + Khaleem Ali + GrenCHAP UPR stakeholder report (Oct 2024) on LGBTIQ+ rights in Grenada: documents the legal and social situation for the UN review, including Sections 430/431 criminal provisions, and GrenCHAP's 15+ years of service to marginalised groups (LGBT+, PLHIV, sex workers, vulnerable youth).

Outright International profile (updated Mar 2026): same-sex conduct criminalised under Sections 430 ('grossly indecent act') and 431 ('unnatural crime'); no legal gender recognition; no anti-discrimination protections; LGBTIQ people face discrimination in housing, education, employment and public services, and fear of prosecution inhibits reporting to police.

US State Dept 2023 report on Grenada: significant human-rights issues include laws criminalising consensual sexual conduct between men, though not enforced; no arbitrary killings, torture or disappearances reported.

records.name: Bahamas
records.summary: The Bahamas demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 1991; tourism-dependent economy with extensive international exposure; no LGR; documented social hostility but no criminalisation and no police-targeting pattern.

sources.summary: The Tribune (27 Apr 2016): Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United launched the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign; BTIU stressed there are no laws protecting transgender and intersex Bahamians, and member Torri Culmer advocates against job termination for trans/intersex workers. For this record: documented absence of trans-specific legal protection plus organised advocacy.

GayLawNet Bahamas law page: on 16 May 1991 consensual same-sex sex was decriminalised (Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act), and in May 1998 the National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson announced the military, prison service and police do not discriminate. For this record: the statutory decriminalisation date plus an official non-discrimination statement.

The Tribune (8 May 2017): Adrian Brown, 24 (Jamaica-born, US-resident), was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being 'targeted and beat up' because he is gay at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival early Saturday, and wants charges laid. For this record: violent targeting of a gay VISITOR during a major tourist event — direct visitor-risk evidence, dated 2017.

records.name: Belize
records.summary: Belize demands real caution. The Court of Appeal struck down the sodomy law in 2016 (Orozco v AG) — the Caribbean's first decriminalisation ruling; Belize has an organised community (UNIBAM) and anti-discrimination employment protection. No LGR; gang violence in Belize City is a general risk.

sources.summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust page documents constitutional challenges to laws criminalising same-sex activity across the Eastern Caribbean, including Belize (the 2016 Orozco ruling decriminalised same-sex conduct in Belize).

UNPR review coverage (2018): Belize accepted 15 of 17 SOGI recommendations — the first CARICOM country to accept that many — pledging legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, police training and SOGI data collection; two rights-equality recommendations 'noted' rather than accepted.

Belize Supreme Court, 10 Aug 2016 (Chief Justice Kenneth Benjamin): colonial-era Section 53 sodomy law struck down as unconstitutional — the challenge LGBT advocate Caleb Orozco filed in 2010; landmark decriminalisation for the country.

Expat overview (2019): after the 2016 ruling — first former British Caribbean colony to overturn its anti-sodomy law — gay travellers have long found Belize friendly, though the rarely-enforced law had fostered intolerance (a 1998 gay-cruise docking protest shows residual hostility).

Live coverage (2013) of the constitutional challenge to Section 53: Unibam's Orozco case tested in Belize City, with day-by-day courtroom dispatches — the litigation that eventually produced the 2016 strike-down.

records.name: Haiti
records.summary:
Haiti is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but the national government has effectively collapsed: gangs control most of the capital (Port-au-Prince), the police are outgunned, and mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition, no protection infrastructure, and no functioning judiciary.

The trans-specific risk is inseparable from the generalised collapse — outing in gang-controlled areas can be lethal. A 2018 official US State Department report described attitudes as hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity, particularly in the capital; freshness confirms trans people remain exposed to vagrancy-law fines with zero protection or hate-crime coverage.

sources.summary: Washington Blade (25 Nov 2019): Charlot Jeudy, president of Kouraj, Haiti's national LGBTQ advocacy organization, was found dead at his home in Port-au-Prince; poisoning reports were unconfirmed by the Blade. ILGALAC issued a mourning statement. The piece cites the US State Department's 2018 report that attitudes in Haiti 'remained hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity and expression, particularly in Port-au-Prince' — a direct climate warning for visibly trans visitors.

HRW World Report 2018 (Haiti chapter): LGBT persons continued to face high levels of discrimination. A June 2017 Senate bill would allow denial of the Certificat de Bonne Vie et Moeurs (a good-conduct certificate employers and universities require) on grounds of homosexuality; in August 2017 the Senate passed a bill banning same-sex marriage and public LGBT advocacy with up to 3 years' prison and a ~US$8,000 fine for parties. Both awaited a Chamber of Deputies vote as of November 2017 — status must be verified before relying on them.
